- Tax Preparer Resume: Examples, Tips, and a Template


Tax preparers perform an essential role for small businesses and individuals, but getting hired takes more than the right skills or education. You need a tax preparer resume that clears the applicant tracking system (ATS) and gives a hiring manager a reason to keep reading.


A strong resume leads with your core credentials and backs them up with relevant work experience and software proficiency. It also includes quantifiable achievements, like the number of returns you’ve processed and your accuracy rate.


This guide covers what to include and how to organize your resume by experience level. You’ll also find a tax preparer resume sample you can build from.


## **Key Points**


- A strong tax preparer resume includes your credentials and certifications alongside your tax, accounting, software, and interpersonal skills.
- Tailor your work experience to the job description as much as you can. Using the exact keywords from the posting can help your resume pass ATS screening and reach a hiring manager.
- Measurable achievements, like accuracy rate or hours saved, tell employers what you’ve accomplished better than a list of skills or tools can.
- Nearly three-quarters (72%) of recruiters[spend less than two minutes](https://zety.com/blog/recruiting-preferences) looking at a resume before deciding whether to move forward. A strong career summary (for experienced candidates) or objective statement (for entry-level candidates) helps capture their attention.


## **What to Include in a Tax Preparer Resume**


Whether you’re applying for tax preparer or tax accountant roles, the resume will look similar. They tend to have the same core sections, but with a different emphasis depending on the job and your experience level.


- **Job title:** At the top of your resume, list a title that matches the role you’re pursuing—for example, “Tax Preparer” or “Tax Accountant.”
- **Contact info:** Below the job title, include your first and last name, email address, and phone number. You could include your full mailing address, too, though listing your city and state is usually sufficient.
- **Career summary or objective:** If you’re experienced in tax preparation or accounting, include a career summary highlighting your background and key accomplishments. If you’re just starting out, write a career objective with your relevant skills and credentials instead.
- **Skills:** Include a section dedicated to your hard and soft skills. Examples include “customer service,” “tax compliance,” or “QuickBooks software.”
- **Experience:** List roles in reverse chronological order. Under each role, include your job title, company name, city and state, and the dates you worked. And note your key responsibilities and quantifiable achievements (e.g., average turnaround time).
- **Education:** A college degree isn’t required to[become a tax preparer](https://www.intuit.com/blog/life-at-intuit/intuit-experts/how-to-become-a-tax-preparer/) , but list what you have. Be sure to include relevant coursework in accounting or taxation, too.
- **Certifications:** Include a section with relevant credentials, like an IRS-issued preparer tax identification number (PTIN), Volunteer Income Tax Assistance (VITA) certification, or a professional certification through the National Association of Tax Professionals (NATP).


Clearing the ATS is a reality of the modern job search. One study found that[71% of employers](https://resumegenius.com/blog/job-hunting/hiring-insights-report) use the technology to filter applications. Here are some tips to help your resume make it through:


- Use simple formatting. That means no fancy fonts and minimal to no graphics or tables.
- Include exact keywords from the job description where they fit your actual experience.
- Submit your resume according to the posting’s instructions (usually as a .docx or PDF).
- Keep your resume to a single page.


## **How to Write Achievement-Driven Experience Bullets**


The experience section on your tax preparer resume shouldn’t read like a series of job descriptions. It should show what you accomplished at each role and how much you contributed.


Start with the job posting. Pull the relevant skills and qualifications that match your own background and weave them into your skills and experience sections. That’s how you tailor the resume to the specific position and give the ATS the language it’s looking for.


Under each role, use three to five bullet points that illustrate your most relevant skills and contributions. Start each with an action verb, name what you did, and end with a result.


The formula: action verb + what you did + metric or quantified result


For example:


- Processed 175 individual/business tax returns per tax season with a 99% accuracy rate
- Identified tax breaks (credits, deductions) to help support and increase average client refund amount by $325
- Addressed and resolved tax-related concerns through in-person client meetings and regular follow-up, leading to a 97% overall satisfaction rate
- Boosted client retention by 27% each tax season via ongoing support and quick turnaround times


Some of the metrics worth tracking for a tax preparer resume include:


- Number of tax returns prepared and completed each season
- Error rate reduction
- Client retention rates
- Number of audits supported
- Average refund secured
- Typical turnaround times (and any improvements)


Not every bullet needs a metric. But the more measurable results you can include, the better. Even 1 per role can go a long way.


*Note: There’s also no need to expose client-identifying details to quantify your results. Leave out any names or other personal information and focus on your achievements instead. Tax preparers work with sensitive information, and hiring managers know it. They also know a resume isn’t the place to prove it by naming names.*


## **Certifications and Software Skills to Highlight**


Split your credentials across two sections: one for education and one for certifications. Under the education section, list any college degrees (associate, bachelor’s, or higher) with the institution name and relevant coursework.


Under Certifications, lead with the credentials most relevant to tax prep work:


- [PTIN](https://www.irs.gov/tax-professionals/ptin-requirements-for-tax-return-preparers)
- [VITA](https://apps.irs.gov/app/vita/) certification
- [Annual Filing Season Program (AFSP)](https://www.irs.gov/tax-professionals/annual-filing-season-program)
- [Enrolled Agent (EA)](https://test-takers.psigov.us/irs)
- [Certified Tax Preparer (CTP)](https://www.nacpb.org/license/certified-tax-professional-license)
- Tax Professional Certificate via[National Association of Tax Professionals (NATP)](https://www.natptax.com/events-education/natp-credential-programs/)
- [Intuit QuickBooks Certified ProAdvisor](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/accountants/training-certification/certification/)
- [Certified Public Accountant (CPA)](https://www.intuit.com/blog/life-at-intuit/intuit-experts/how-to-become-a-cpa/) license


For each credential, include the issuing organization and the year you earned it. If the credential has an expiration date, include that as well.


### **Software Proficiency**


Employers also look for candidates who understand e-filing platforms and tax preparation software. That includes:


- IRS’ e-filing system
- Intuit Pro Series
- TaxAct
- [Intuit QuickBooks](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/)


Name the software you’ve used under your skills section, as well as any relevant work experience. Include a proficiency level for each. “Proficient,” “advanced,” or “expert” reads more professionally than “intermediate” or “beginner.”


## **Tax Preparer Resume Example**


Here’s what an entry-level tax preparer resume looks like when you put the pieces together:


**Tax Preparer**


Jane Smith


jane.smith@gmail.com | 555-123-4567 | Seattle, WA 98103


**Career Summary**


Certified tax preparer with two years of experience preparing tax returns for individual and small business clients. Maintained a 100% accuracy rate across 130 returns per tax season, while helping ensure clients received the maximum allowable refund. Fluent in tax law, as well as industry-standard software like Intuit QuickBooks and Excel.


**Skills**


Tax compliance


Tax returns


Tax credits and deductions


GAAP familiarity


Foreign and domestic tax regulations


Tax software (Intuit Pro Series, TaxAct)


Accounting software (QuickBooks)


Accounting practices


Data analysis


Problem-solving


Collaboration


Customer service


**Work Experience**


Tax Preparer


Jones Accounting Firm | Seattle, WA | June 2024 to Present


- Prepared 130 tax returns per tax season for individuals and businesses
- Helped ensure compliance with state and federal tax regulations
- Coordinated with senior tax professionals to improve client retention rates by 30% year-over-year
- Analyzed clients’ financial and tax records alongside current tax law to increase average refund amount by $375 per client


**Education**


Bachelor of Arts in Business Administration and Accounting | Graduated: 2024


Washington State University | Seattle, WA


Relevant coursework: General Accounting, Tax Planning, Corporate Taxation


**Certifications**


Certified Tax Preparer (CTP) | Consortia Accounting School | Completed: 2024


Intuit QuickBooks ProAdvisor | Completed: 2025


If you’re considering a related role, like tax accountant, the same resume template largely applies. The main difference is that a tax accountant or CPA resume needs to emphasize different skills and credentials. They’d typically put the spotlight more on advisory or auditing services alongside tax assistance, for example.

## **FAQs**


###


Include a skills and an experience section on your resume. Within the skills section, list your core capabilities or qualifications, like “tax return preparation” or “customer service.” Then, under each role, list your most relevant tasks and contributions in three to five bullets. Ideally, each bullet will also include a quantifiable metric, like the number of returns filed or accuracy rates.


###


By law, you must minimally have an IRS-issued PTIN to prepare federal tax returns as a paid preparer. So, include that on your resume. Other credentials to list are your EA status, CPA license, AFSP program, VITA certification, Intuit QuickBooks certification, and any other professional tax prep certificates you’ve earned. You could also list relevant coursework in accounting or tax law under your education.


###


Use aggregate numbers and role-based descriptions instead of client names or identifying details. Metrics like turnaround time, accuracy rate, number of returns filed, and client retention rate quantify your impact without pointing to anyone specific. When you need to describe the type of client you worked with, use categories—“small business clients,” “high-net-worth individuals,” “multi-state filers”—rather than names or industries specific enough to identify a real customer.
